Renal and Genitourinary Disorders

Male Genital Problems

Male genital complaints are a mix of anatomy, infection, vascular compromise, and surgical emergencies. The ED priority is recognizing the five time-sensitive GU emergencies while still treating common infections and painful benign conditions.

Board trap: Acute scrotal pain is torsion until proven otherwise; a positive UA, present cremasteric reflex, or “Prehn sign” does not safely rule it out.

INTRODUCTION

The chapter covers acute infectious and structural/anatomic male GU disorders. High-risk emergencies are testicular torsion, Fournier gangrene, paraphimosis, ischemic priapism, and significant GU trauma.

ANATOMY

PENIS

The corpora cavernosa provide erectile rigidity, the corpus spongiosum surrounds the urethra, and penile vascular/lymphatic anatomy explains edema, priapism, fracture, infection spread, and malignancy drainage.

SCROTUM

Scrotal skin and dartos muscle change with puberty and can swell dramatically from local or systemic disease. Scrotal wall findings must be separated from testicular, epididymal, spermatic cord, and inguinal processes.

TESTES

The testis is suspended by the spermatic cord and anchored by the tunica vaginalis. A bell-clapper deformity permits torsion around the cord. A horizontal lie is a torsion risk clue.

EPIDIDYMIS AND VAS DEFERENS

The epididymis sits posteriorly and becomes focally tender early in epididymitis before swelling merges with the testis in epididymo-orchitis.

PROSTATE

The prostate can drive urinary obstruction and infection. Acute prostatitis causes systemic illness plus LUTS and a tender/boggy gland; do not massage an acutely infected prostate.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Examine penis, foreskin, glans, shaft, scrotum, testes, epididymis, spermatic cord, inguinal canal, cremasteric reflex, and perineum. Return the foreskin after exam to avoid iatrogenic paraphimosis.

DISORDERS OF THE SCROTUM

An acute scrotum is acute pain or swelling. Torsion and Fournier gangrene are the time-sensitive killers/testis-threatening diagnoses.

SCROTAL EDEMA

Edema can be from contact dermatitis, bites, idiopathic scrotal edema, systemic edema, or contiguous penile swelling. Ultrasound can distinguish wall thickening from intratesticular pathology.

SCROTAL ABSCESS

Superficial follicular abscess may be incised and drained, but deeper abscess, urethral source, or indistinct mass requires ultrasound/urology. Early Fournier must remain in the differential.

FOURNIER’S GANGRENE

Fournier is necrotizing polymicrobial infection of perineal/genital/perianal fascia. Pain may precede dramatic skin findings; diabetes, immunocompromise, alcoholism, obesity, and delayed treatment increase mortality.

CLINICAL FEATURES AND DIAGNOSIS

Look for severe pain, edema, toxicity, crepitus, bullae, necrosis, foul odor, or perineal source. Imaging can show gas or dirty shadowing but must not delay surgical consultation.

TREATMENT

Treatment is immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics, resuscitation, and aggressive surgical debridement; hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive only.

Figure 93-4

Fournier gangrene of the scrotum.

DISORDERS OF THE PENIS

BALANOPOSTHITIS

Balanitis/posthitis cause pain, erythema, discharge, and swelling. Treat hygiene problems, Candida with topical azole/nystatin, bacterial cellulitis with antibiotics, and evaluate STI when urethritis features exist.

PHIMOSIS

Phimosis is inability to retract foreskin. Physiologic childhood phimosis often resolves; pathologic phimosis follows inflammation/scarring and may improve with topical steroid or require urology.

PARAPHIMOSIS

Paraphimosis is trapped retracted foreskin behind the glans with edema and venous congestion. It is a urologic emergency: compress edema, provide analgesia/dorsal penile block, reduce promptly, and consult urology if unsuccessful.

Tintinalli source

Figure 93-5

Phimosis and paraphimosis.

ENTRAPMENT INJURIES

Hair tourniquets and rings can cause ischemia. Remove the constricting object while protecting skin; delayed cases may need urology or specialty tools.

Tintinalli source

Figure 93-6

Hair entrapped behind the coronal sulcus.

FRACTURE OF THE PENIS

Penile fracture is rupture of tunica albuginea after blunt injury to an erect penis, often with snap/pop, immediate pain, detumescence, and swelling. Treat with urgent urology and surgical repair; evaluate urethral injury if blood at meatus/hematuria.

PEYRONIE’S DISEASE

Peyronie is chronic fibrous plaque causing curvature and painful erections. It is not the acute fracture emergency but can mimic chronic penile pain/curvature complaints.

PRIAPISM

Priapism is erection lasting beyond sexual stimulation. Ischemic priapism is painful low-flow emergency; nonischemic is high-flow, often less painful after trauma.

ASPIRATION AND IRRIGATION OF CORPORA CAVERNOSA

For ischemic priapism, give analgesia, aspirate/irrigate corpora, and inject phenylephrine with monitoring. Sickle cell priapism also needs analgesia, hydration, oxygen as indicated, and urology/hematology.

PENILE CARCINOMA

Penile carcinoma can present as nonhealing lesion, mass, ulcer, bleeding, or phimosis-associated abnormality. Arrange urgent urologic follow-up rather than treating as simple balanitis indefinitely.

DISORDERS OF THE TESTES AND EPIDIDYMIS

TESTICULAR TORSION

Torsion causes spermatic cord twisting and ischemia, peaking in neonates and puberty. Salvage falls quickly after 6 hours and becomes poor by 24 hours, so torsion is the first diagnosis to exclude.

Tintinalli source

Table 93-1

Differential diagnosis of acute scrotal pain.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding or horizontal testis, and absent cremasteric reflex support torsion. None of the bedside signs reliably rules it out.

DIAGNOSIS

Obvious torsion is clinical and should go directly to urology/exploration. Equivocal cases get Doppler ultrasound, but partial or intermittent torsion can have misleading flow.

TREATMENT

Immediate urologic consultation is definitive. Manual detorsion can be attempted while preparing surgery, usually “opening a book”; success does not eliminate need for orchiopexy.

APPENDAGEAL TORSION

Appendage torsion is slower, milder, and may show blue-dot sign. If Doppler confirms normal testicular flow and torsion is excluded, treat with NSAIDs, rest, ice, and scrotal support.

EPIDIDYMITIS

Epididymitis has gradual onset scrotal/epididymal pain that may progress to epididymo-orchitis. Younger/sexually active patients need STI coverage; older or insertive anal intercourse/urinary tract abnormality raises enteric organism risk.

CLINICAL FEATURES AND DIAGNOSIS

Find focal epididymal tenderness, swelling, urinary symptoms, fever, discharge, and risk history. Severe swelling can mimic torsion or abscess; do not let a UTI story end the torsion workup when the exam is high risk.

TREATMENT

Treat with syndrome-based antibiotics, scrotal support, analgesia, STI partner management, and follow-up. Admit fever/toxicity, abscess concern, inability to tolerate PO, or severe comorbidity.

Tintinalli source

Table 93-2

Empiric outpatient treatment of epididymitis and epididymo-orchitis.

ORCHITIS

Isolated orchitis is rare and often viral such as mumps; bacterial orchitis usually accompanies epididymitis. Use ultrasound when torsion or abscess remains possible.

TESTICULAR MALIGNANCY

Any unexplained firm/nodular testicular mass is malignancy until proven otherwise. Infection can coexist with or obscure tumor, so ensure follow-up and ultrasound.

ACUTE PROSTATITIS

CLINICAL FEATURES AND DIAGNOSIS

Acute prostatitis causes fever, chills, malaise, pelvic/perineal pain, dysuria, frequency, retention, and tender/boggy prostate. Diagnosis is clinical with UA/culture support; avoid prostatic massage.

TREATMENT

Treat with antibiotics that penetrate the prostate, analgesia, fluids, and admission for sepsis, retention, immunocompromise, vomiting, or abscess concern.

DISORDERS OF THE URETHRA

URETHRAL FOREIGN BODIES

Urethral foreign bodies may present with pain, bleeding, retention, infection, or embarrassment-delayed history. Avoid blind extraction that worsens trauma; involve urology for endoscopic or operative removal.
